Apple's annual September iPhone launch event is still about two months away, but this year will be different. In September, Apple won't unveil its entire iPhone lineup at once—it will only debut the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and a brand-new foldable iPhone first.

The iPhone Lineup Keeps Expanding

Over the past few years, the annual iPhone lineup has gradually expanded. Not long ago, only three new models would launch each year: the iPhone 11, iPhone 11 Pro, and iPhone 11 Pro Max. By 2020, with the addition of the iPhone 12 mini, the number of models launched each year increased to four. By 2022, the iPhone 12 mini was replaced by the iPhone 14 Plus, which was later succeeded by the iPhone Air.

With the arrival of the iPhone 16e, the number of models launched each year has further increased to five. Once the iPhone Ultra arrives, the annual iPhone lineup will expand to six models. With so many models—unveiling them all at once would certainly make for a very crowded stage.

Therefore, Apple has decided to adopt a phased launch strategy.

Two iPhone Launch Events: Fall and Spring

The iPhone 18 series will include six models: iPhone 18, iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone 18e, iPhone Air 2, and iPhone Ultra.

The logic behind this phased strategy is clear: flagship models debut in the fall, while mid-range and entry-level models appear in the spring. The specific arrangement is as follows:

  • Fall 2026: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone Ultra
  • Spring 2027: iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, iPhone Air 2

Whenever the iPhone lineup expanded to four models, that fourth model always performed disappointingly in terms of sales—whether it was the iPhone mini or the iPhone Plus. So Apple believes it makes perfect sense to clearly delineate the product lineup and give the extra model its own moment in the spotlight.

However, when it comes to the iPhone 18, the situation will be slightly different. Reports suggest Apple is working to unify the production processes for the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, so the differences between the two phones may be significantly narrowed.

It's not yet clear whether this approach will bring major upgrades to the iPhone 18e or result in downgrades to the iPhone 18—but the distinction between the two phones may ultimately come down to details like the display panel and camera.

Summary

In summary, assuming the iPhone Air ultimately isn't discontinued (I certainly hope that won't happen)—this is the new landscape for the iPhone lineup going forward. Three models in the fall, three models in the spring. The ultimate goal is to allow Apple to better spread out its launch schedule and deliver products to the right consumers.

Another possible outcome is that the average selling price of iPhones will rise, because any consumer wanting to ride the wave of new hardware will have no choice but to buy the iPhone 18 Pro, rather than a cheaper model.

Whether the phased rollout can truly drive sales across all models remains to be seen, but these are the initial observations.

What are your thoughts on Apple's phased iPhone launch approach? Will you buy a new iPhone in the fall, or wait until the spring? Feel free to share your opinions in the comments section.
